items.title: The two-phone Game Boy link: the app's half
items.detail: cBoy's half of the link cable is built and tested (commit 5c73e93): a byte takes a real cable's time, the console being driven waits for the other one, and two phones can swap bytes over one agreement that cannot drift, with a give-up so a bad connection can never freeze a game. docs/CBOY_NIGHT.md spells out the three things the app must do. Do them using the online-play connection the app already has (crates/emulator-bridge/src/netplay/, uniffi_online.rs, and the online-play screens in native/ios), so two players running Game Boy or Game Boy Color games on cBoy can link: trade Pokemon, play Tetris head to head. The player-facing part must be plain: one clear way to start a link with the other phone, and a plain line if the other phone isn't running cBoy or the connection drops. Prove it with two engine instances talking to each other in one test process (a byte exchange through the real libretro entry points of a host-built cBoy, both directions, with internal and external clock, plus the give-up). Do not edit cores/continuum-gb: if cBoy needs a change, write it into the report and work around it.

items.title: The EEPROM save in Sampras Tennis 96, and every other Mega Drive EEPROM cartridge
items.detail: Last night found that the save item named the wrong game: Pete Sampras Tennis 96 is the one with an EEPROM, and its BlastEm cartridge entry needs that cartridge's real checksum and EEPROM layout, which were not guessed. MAME's software lists are CC0-licensed data: hash/megadriv.xml in the MAME repository lists each Mega Drive cartridge's CRC32 and SHA1 and its save hardware. Read the entries from there (fetch the one file into scratch, never commit it), add the cartridge entry to BlastEm's cartridge list in scripts/patches/blastem-continuum-memory.patch (or a new blastem-*.patch), and check every other EEPROM Mega Drive cartridge in that list against BlastEm's (the Codemasters Micro Machines games, the EA sports games, the Sega ones), adding any that are missing. Unit-test that the patch applies and the entries parse. Say in the report which games now save that did not.

items.title: Mesen 2 as the second SNES choice
items.detail: Last night checked and did not offer it, for a good reason: everything the Continuum Mesen patch gives the NES (memory for RAM search and achievements, cheats, and letting the app own the battery save) is written NES-only, so SNES players would have lost all three. Extend the patch (scripts/patches/mesen2-nes-memory-cheats-saves.patch, or a new mesen2-snes-*.patch) so the SNES gets the same three: the console's work RAM and the cartridge's save RAM exposed to the app, typed SNES cheat codes (Game Genie and Pro Action Replay) reaching Mesen's own cheat code, and the battery save owned by the app like every other core. Build Mesen 2 for the host, boot open-licensed SNES homebrew through the engine, and prove a battery save round-trips, a save state round-trips and a cheat changes memory. Compare its speed with bsnes on the host and write the numbers down. Then offer it as the second core for SNES (bsnes stays the default). If one of the three cannot be made to hold tonight, do not offer it, and say exactly what is left.

items.title: Sega CD: changing discs, and the RAM-cart saves
items.detail: Last night found that BlastEm registers no libretro disc interface and has no hook for changing a disc, and that libretro's one save region is already used by the Sega CD's internal backup memory. Add the disc interface to BlastEm's libretro front end in a Continuum patch so the app's existing 'Next disc' control (the one PS1 uses) works for multi-disc Sega CD games, and store the backup RAM cartridge (the add-on save cartridge) as its own file next to the internal one, loaded and saved with it. A Sega CD game needs a BIOS nobody here has, so prove what can be proved without one (the interface's calls, the disc list from a .m3u, the cartridge file being created, saved and reloaded) and say plainly that a real disc swap needs the phone.

items.title: Continuum's own 32X start-up code, so 32X games need no BIOS files
items.detail: Today a 32X game asks for 32X_M_BIOS.bin and 32X_S_BIOS.bin. Last night's report says where Continuum's own start-up code would hook in and what it has to do (set up the two SH-2 processors, check and copy the cartridge's SH-2 program as its header describes, hand over, and the handshake the Mega Drive side waits for). Write it as Continuum's own code, assembled with an SH-2 assembler you build from source in scratch (GNU binutils builds for sh-elf in a few minutes), and prove it by booting open-licensed 32X homebrew in a host build of BlastEm. No time box: keep at it until it boots real 32X homebrew in the host build. Never ship start-up code that has not booted something. Only if it is truly impossible here (name the reason; slow or hard is not a reason) keep the existing needs-the-BIOS line exactly as it is, so nothing gets worse, and write what you learned into the report.
